title: Scree-plot cliff and cumulative variance
alt: The normalized scree curve drops sharply and then enters a flat tail, while cumulative variance gradually approaches one hundred percent.
caption: Read the two curves in principal-component order: beyond the cliff, each eigenvalue contributes little additional variance, while cumulative variance continues to rise monotonically. The elbow suggests candidate dimensionalities but does not determine a unique cutoff; the plotted coordinates illustrate the normalized relation on page 6 and are not empirical data.

annotations.label: Marginal gain decreases beyond the cliff

questionDistractors.text: After the cliff the eigenvalues decrease, so the cumulative variance curve must turn downward too.
questionDistractors.explanation: Cumulative explained variance is a normalized partial sum of nonnegative eigenvalues. Smaller eigenvalues add less, but cannot subtract previously accumulated variance.

questionDistractors.text: The flat tail means all remaining PCs have exactly zero variance and can be removed without reconstruction error.
questionDistractors.explanation: A nearly flat tail means similar small eigenvalues, not necessarily zero eigenvalues. Removing directions with nonzero variance still creates reconstruction error.

questionDistractors.text: The cliff uniquely identifies the true neural dimensionality and guarantees preservation of all behavioral information.
questionDistractors.explanation: An elbow suggests candidate cutoffs. Noise, preprocessing, and analysis goals affect dimensionality selection, and retained activity variance does not guarantee retained behavioral information.

questionAnswer: Individual eigenvalues fall after the cliff while cumulative variance keeps increasing toward 100%.

title: Morris–Lecar nullclines and the relaxation cycle
alt: A voltage–recovery phase plane with an N-shaped voltage nullcline, an S-shaped recovery nullcline, an unstable intersection, and a relaxation trajectory encircling that intersection.
caption: The intersection of the two nullclines is a candidate equilibrium. Here it is unstable, so the trajectory moves slowly along the outer attracting branches of the V-nullcline and jumps rapidly to the other branch near each fold. Long portions of the loop represent slow recovery, whereas nearly horizontal crossings represent fast voltage transitions. The curves are a normalized schematic of the mechanisms on Pages 3–4.
questionAnswer: Slow recovery along outer branches alternates with fast voltage jumps near folds; the unstable intersection does not trap the trajectory.

questionDistractors.text: The nullclines are successive segments of one actual trajectory, and their stable intersection forces every initial state around the loop.
questionDistractors.explanation: Nullclines are sets where derivatives vanish, not successive time segments. The illustrated intersection is unstable and the loop surrounds it.

questionDistractors.text: Nearly horizontal crossings keep voltage fixed while recovery jumps rapidly; the outer branches instead show voltage rising at a constant speed.
questionDistractors.explanation: Voltage is on the horizontal axis. Near-horizontal crossings mainly change voltage, whereas branch segments reflect slow recovery rather than constant-speed voltage growth.

questionDistractors.text: The loop is determined only by the initial state; both derivatives vanish everywhere on it, so circulation needs no fast or slow changes.
questionDistractors.explanation: Zero values of both derivatives imply stationarity, not circulation. The cycle requires nonzero flow along its path.

title: Three fates of an eigenvalue-one integrator
alt: After the command ends, a mode whose eigenvalue is less than one decays, a mode equal to one persists, and a mode greater than one grows.
caption: After input is removed, the fate of the same initial mode amplitude depends only on \(1-\lambda\): when \(\lambda <1\) it leaks; when \(\lambda =1\) the restoring coefficient in the derivative vanishes and memory persists; when \(\lambda >1\) a small deviation grows. Thus \(\det(I-W)=0\) guarantees only an integrating mode, and the stability of all remaining modes must still be checked.
questionAnswer: After input ends, the mode decays, persists, or grows according to its eigenvalue; one integrating mode does not stabilize every other direction.

questionDistractors.text: The curves differ only in initial amplitude; once input ends, every mode of a linear network must decay with the same time constant.
questionDistractors.explanation: The connectivity eigenvalue relative to leak differs across the curves, changing growth rates; initial amplitude is not the sole difference.

questionDistractors.text: An eigenvalue above one produces stronger restoring force, so the growing curve should decay fastest and only values below one amplify errors.
questionDistractors.explanation: This reverses the sign: above one, recurrent feedback exceeds leak and the full mode has a positive growth rate.

questionDistractors.text: The persistent middle curve proves stability of the entire network under every perturbation, eliminating any need to check other eigenvalues or transverse modes.
questionDistractors.explanation: Persistence of one mode only establishes absence of leak in that direction; other directions can still decay or grow.

title: From population activity to closed-loop BMI
alt: Population neural activity passes through GPFA latent inference, cross-day alignment, and a shared BMI decoder to produce cursor feedback, which then affects subsequent neural activity.
caption: Observed activity is first compressed by GPFA into daily latent coordinates, then \(A_{d}\) aligns those coordinates to a shared space and passes them to shared decoder B. Decoder output changes cursor feedback, which in turn changes subsequent neural activity. Cross-day stability therefore means that a low-dimensional mapping is transferable; it does not require each neuron's loading to remain fixed.
questionAnswer: Daily latent coordinates are aligned before shared decoding, and cursor feedback returns to affect subsequent neural activity.

questionDistractors.text: Alignment merely overlays plots after feedback and never changes the coordinates given to the shared decoder.
questionDistractors.explanation: The alignment map sits between latent inference and the shared decoder and therefore changes the decoder’s input coordinates.

questionDistractors.text: A shared decoder rules out participant adaptation; the feedback arrow merely displays output and later activity must retain the open-loop calibration distribution.
questionDistractors.explanation: Feedback can alter strategy and neural distributions. Shared parameters do not make the closed-loop system passive or open loop.

questionDistractors.text: A transferable cross-day map requires every neuron’s loading to remain permanently fixed; changing one loading makes stable latent decoding impossible.
questionDistractors.explanation: Population structure can remain alignable despite individual loading changes; stable latent decoding does not require fixed single-cell identity.

title: First-passage paths in drift–diffusion
alt: Two noisy accumulation trajectories leave the same starting point and first reach the positive and negative decision boundaries, respectively.
caption: Each path begins at bias b, accumulates noisy evidence step by step, and stops the first time it reaches +B or −B. The endpoint determines choice and the horizontal coordinate determines decision time. Under identical task parameters, noise can carry the two trajectories to different boundaries; a trajectory must not be averaged further after crossing before a decision is assigned.
questionAnswer: With the same parameters, noise can reach opposite boundaries; first-crossing sign gives choice and crossing time gives decision time.

questionDistractors.text: Choice is determined by final average height; after the first crossing, continue accumulating and classify the trial using the average of both paths.
questionDistractors.explanation: A first-passage decision ends at the initial crossing; later samples or averages over other trials cannot redefine that decision.

questionDistractors.text: The positive boundary means a slow response and the negative boundary a fast response of the same choice, while horizontal position represents stimulus strength.
questionDistractors.explanation: Boundary sign identifies the two choices, and time is read on the horizontal axis; this interpretation swaps their meanings.

questionDistractors.text: Opposite boundaries prove different mean evidence; at fixed coherence, noise can change timing but never the direction of choice.
questionDistractors.explanation: Fixed mean evidence does not fix the noise path. Stochastic accumulation can change both timing and the first boundary reached.

title: TD error transfers from reward to a predictive cue
alt: Three timelines compare dopamine prediction error around the cue and reward deadline before learning, after learning, and when reward is omitted.
caption: Compare the same trial row by row. Before learning, only unexpected reward produces positive \(\delta\). After the cue–reward relation is learned, positive \(\delta\) moves earlier to the cue and is nearly zero when reward arrives on time. If reward is omitted at the deadline, negative \(\delta\) appears then. This pattern of signs supports prediction error rather than a pure reward response.
questionAnswer: Learning shifts positive error to the cue; expected reward gives little error, while omission gives negative error at the expected time.

questionDistractors.text: After learning, the cue and the predicted reward retain equally large positive errors because each is independently counted as a new reward.
questionDistractors.explanation: An already predicted reward no longer carries the same positive surprise.

questionDistractors.text: Omission merely removes a positive response and never produces a below-baseline dip.
questionDistractors.explanation: The figure explicitly shows a negative error at the expected reward time.

questionDistractors.text: The omission dip precedes the cue, so learning the interval between cue and reward is unnecessary for generating the illustrated response.
questionDistractors.explanation: The dip occurs at the predicted reward deadline, which requires temporal prediction.

title: The agent–environment loop and a one-step Bellman backup
alt: The agent selects an action from the current state, the environment returns reward and a next state, and a one-step Bellman target updates the action value backward.
caption: In the forward interaction, policy maps \(s_{t}\) to \(a_{t}\), after which the environment samples r and \(s_{t+1}\). The backup then uses \(r+\gamma  \max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\) to update current \(Q(s_{t},a_{t})\). A dashed path carries \(s_{t+1}\) into the next cycle, showing that the Markov transition and value backup are connected steps pointing in opposite directions.
questionAnswer: The environment supplies reward and a successor state; a one-step target updates the current action value, and the successor starts the next interaction.

questionDistractors.text: The Bellman backup directly changes environmental transition probabilities to force movement along the highest-value path.
questionDistractors.explanation: The backup updates a value estimate rather than rewriting the environment's transition mechanism.

questionDistractors.text: Before choosing its action, the agent already observes that action's actual reward and successor state, so the illustrated target requires no environmental interaction.
questionDistractors.explanation: The actual reward and successor are observed after the action and environmental response.

questionDistractors.text: Reward updates every action in the successor state while leaving the executed current action's value unchanged.
questionDistractors.explanation: The illustrated update targets the value of the action actually taken in the current state.

title: Hopfield basins: descent does not guarantee correct recall
alt: A cue near the target descends to the stored pattern under asynchronous updates, whereas an ambiguous cue lowers energy as well but descends to a spurious minimum
caption: With symmetric weights, a zero diagonal, and asynchronous updates, both paths make E nonincreasing, but the cue's basin determines the endpoint. A cue near the target can complete to \(\xi ^{\mu }\), whereas crosstalk may draw an ambiguous cue into a mixture. Energy descent, reaching a fixed point, and correct recall are distinct: low energy alone does not imply that the state is already stable, and a fixed point may encode a spurious memory.
questionAnswer: Both paths can lower energy yet enter target and spurious basins respectively; dynamical convergence is therefore distinct from correct recall.

questionDistractors.text: The path to the spurious attractor must contain an energy increase, or an incorrect memory would be unreachable.
questionDistractors.explanation: Under symmetric asynchronous dynamics, a wrong attractor can also be reached without increasing energy.

questionDistractors.text: Because both paths use the same symmetric weights, every initial cue must end at one unique stored pattern, regardless of its similarity to other memories.
questionDistractors.explanation: One network can have several basins, and the initial cue influences the final state.

questionDistractors.text: Minimum energy automatically identifies the requested target, making a stable mixture a correct recall.
questionDistractors.explanation: Energy does not contain an independent label for the requested target identity.

title: The offline replay channel in Teacher–Student–Notebook
alt: Teacher trains Student online, Student activity is stored together with a sparse Notebook code, and after Notebook completion, V reconstructs the Student pattern for offline replay.
caption: During online learning, Teacher generates training experiences, and each Student pattern \(z^{\mu }\) is stored together with its Notebook code \(\xi ^{\mu }\). During retrieval, the Notebook first completes a partial cue and then uses V to compute \(\widetilde{z}_i=\sum _jV_{ij}\xi _{j}\). The dashed replay path returns the reconstructed activity to Student, allowing Student to continue learning while Teacher is absent.
questionAnswer: The Notebook completes the cue and reconstructs Student activity through the readout, enabling replay-based learning while the Teacher is absent.

questionDistractors.text: Offline replay must first obtain a fresh online Teacher sample; the Notebook cannot supply a learning target itself.
questionDistractors.explanation: The illustrated replay path allows reconstructed activity to be used without the Teacher present.

questionDistractors.text: The readout maps all Notebook codes to one identical activity pattern, so storing distinct episode–Student pairings is unnecessary for the depicted reconstruction.
questionDistractors.explanation: Reconstruction depends on paired storage rather than collapsing every experience to one target.

questionDistractors.text: Notebook completion proves the Student has learned the true environmental rule and needs no further update.
questionDistractors.explanation: Completion supplies a replay sample; learning a generalizable rule still depends on Student training.
